The Striped eel catfish, Plotosus lineatus, is a common marine species in the Indo-West Pacific, known for its distinctive striped patterning and venomous spines. Field surveys along coastal seagrass beds have yielded important life-history data on this species. The ultimate total length reported for Plotosus lineatus reaches 35.2 cm [Li = 35.2 cm], a size that characterizes the largest adults captured in the wild. Studies of growth trajectories indicate that individuals first attain sexual maturity at a significantly smaller size; the total length at puberty has been measured at 16.9 cm [Lp = 16.9 cm], with some earlier accounts by Vijayanand et al. suggesting a slightly lower value. This threshold marks a critical transition in the species' ontogeny. Reproductive ecology in Plotosus lineatus is closely tied to thermal conditions. Under a stable experimental regime maintained at 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 41.8 grams [Wwp = approximately 41.8 grams], a value derived from established length-weight relationships that reflect the somatic condition necessary for the onset of gonadal activity. Understanding these size metrics provides a baseline for assessing population health across this species' expansive geographic range.

Embryonic development and the earliest life stages of Plotosus lineatus are characterized by a brief incubation period and very small size at emergence. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C] hatch after a short duration of 9 days [ab = 9 days], a period typical for tropical catfishes with demersal, adhesive eggs. The newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are notably minute; the wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], a value reflecting the small egg diameter of roughly 1.25 mm. This extremely low mass at eclosion places the species among those producing large numbers of very small offspring. The larvae remain endotrophic for a brief phase, absorbing their yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The rapid development from fertilised ovum to a free-swimming, exogenously feeding larva in just over a week is an adaptation that likely reduces the window of vulnerability to predation during the most fragile stage of the life cycle, allowing the prolarvae to disperse into adjacent habitats before their yolk is fully exhausted.

Adult body size and reproductive output in Plotosus lineatus reveal a pattern of high fecundity characteristic of many marine catfishes. The ultimate wet weight achieved by large, reproductively active adults is 412.6 grams [Wwi = 412.6 grams], a mass that substantially exceeds that of many sympatric plotosids and reflects the culmination of somatic growth over a prolonged juvenile phase. This substantial body size supports a considerable reproductive potential. At a water temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], individual females are capable of producing approximately 5753 eggs over the course of a typical spawning season, with an average of about 1.5 spawning events within that annual period [F_R_i = about 1.5 spawning events within that annual period]. This relatively high output is fueled by the energetic reserves accumulated during the adult growth phase. Comparisons with related plotosid catfishes indicate that Plotosus lineatus invests heavily in concentrated spawning efforts rather than spreading reproduction across many small events, a life-history tactic that aligns with its role as a nest-guarding species in the shallow coastal environment.

Lifespan and longevity estimates for Plotosus lineatus are derived from both field mark-recapture studies and captive observations. Under the same thermal regime maintained at 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], the maximum documented lifespan for this species reaches 7 years [am = 7 years], although earlier accounts by Vijayanand et al. suggest a considerably shorter duration, possibly reflecting differences between wild and laboratory conditions. This longevity of 7 years is relatively extended for a fish that matures at a body length of approximately 17 cm, and it implies a significant post-maturity reproductive lifespan. The species exhibits a semelparous or iteroparous pattern depending on local environmental pressures, but data from consistent environments indicate that most adults survive for several spawning seasons. The attainment of such an age is noteworthy given the intense predation pressure on juvenile eel catfish, particularly during the early benthic juvenile phase. The slow accumulation of body mass, culminating in an ultimate wet weight of 412.6 grams, combined with a long lifespan, positions Plotosus lineatus as a relatively slow-living teleost within its family, with life-history trade-offs that favor somatic persistence over rapid turnover.

A comparative perspective on Plotosus lineatus reveals how its life history parameters align with those of other members of the family Plotosidae. The species' ultimate total length of 35.2 cm [Li = 35.2 cm] is modest relative to some congeneric species, yet it supports a reproductive strategy characterized by high fecundity. The juvenile phase begins with a wet weight at birth of merely 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], representing an extreme contrast to the 412.6 gram [Wwi = 412.6 gram] adult maximum, illustrating a body mass increase of over 400,000-fold. During this growth trajectory, the onset of puberty occurs at a wet weight of 41.8 grams [Wwp = 41.8 grams], a threshold that corresponds to roughly 10 percent of the ultimate wet weight. The incubation period of 9 days [ab = 9 days] at 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C] is among the shortest recorded for marine catfishes, a trait that facilitates rapid larval dispersal. The 7-year maximum lifespan (7 years) [am = 7 years] recorded at 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C] underscores a life-history strategy that balances delayed maturity with high per-capita fecundity, ensuring population persistence in variable and predation-rich coastal ecosystems.
